context.concept_name: Binding request bodies to typed models

coverage.learning_objective: Declare JSON bodies: add one typed create body.

required_facts.statement: Define a BaseModel subclass and annotate a handler parameter with that model to bind a structured JSON request body.
FastAPI reads the JSON body, converts compatible values, validates the declared model and passes the model instance to the handler.
Path-declared parameters bind from the path, scalar parameters generally bind from the query, and model parameters bind from the body, so these inputs can coexist in one operation.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order-creation request contains a structured JSON object, while its URL may also identify a parent resource and supply a scalar query setting. Those inputs can coexist without sharing one binding source.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Define a BaseModel subclass and annotate a handler parameter with that model to bind a structured JSON request body.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: FastAPI reads the JSON body, converts compatible values, validates the declared model and passes the model instance to the handler. Path-declared parameters bind from the path, scalar parameters generally bind from the query, and model parameters bind from the body, so these inputs can coexist in one operation.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: For a combined operation, draw a source table: identifier from the path, ordinary scalar option generally from the query, structured model from the JSON body. FastAPI can supply them together because their declarations identify different input roles. In the model column, write the sequence of reading JSON, converting compatible values, validating the shape and supplying a model instance. That sequence explains why the handler receives a model rather than merely an assumed-valid body. It also keeps a body field from being mistaken for a query parameter with the same conceptual name. Review the source and shape together when explaining the operation contract.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Define an OrderInput BaseModel and annotate the body parameter with it. FastAPI reads the JSON body, converts compatible values, validates the model and passes a model instance to the handler. Compare this with a path-declared customer identifier and an ordinary scalar query option: those bind from the path and generally from the query, respectively. Draw the body as one structured input rather than scattering its fields into assumed query parameters. Then trace a request from body bytes to validated model to handler argument. The model instance is the result of body binding and validation, not simply the untouched JSON data. Keeping source and declared shape together lets you explain where each part of the operation's input comes from.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A structured model parameter binds from the body; it is not the same input declaration as an ordinary scalar query parameter.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Declare JSON bodies: add one typed create body.

practice_anchor.objective: Add a body parameter annotated with OrderInput to the supplied order-creation handler, preserving its existing customer identifier and scalar query option.
practice_anchor.success: The handler declares one structured body using OrderInput. The customer identifier remains bound from the path, and the ordinary scalar option remains bound from the query.

live_code.required_skill: Use a BaseModel subclass as a handler parameter annotation to declare a structured JSON body.
allowed_syntax: model field annotations using str and int
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an OrderInput BaseModel subclass and an order-creation handler with the running example's customer identifier in the route path and ordinary scalar query option. Leave the structured body parameter undeclared.
live_code.observable_success: Code inspection shows body: OrderInput in the handler signature without changing the existing path and query declarations. The learner identifies that FastAPI reads the JSON body, converts compatible values, validates OrderInput and supplies its instance as body.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the OrderInput BaseModel subclass beside the handler signature, with annotations identifying the customer identifier as path input, the ordinary scalar option as query input and body: OrderInput as structured JSON body input.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Structured bodies are distinct from URL inputs.
Stay within the current objective: Declare JSON bodies. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Determine body binding.

coverage.learning_objective: Release yield dependency resources: provide and close one request resource.

required_facts.statement: A dependency with yield acquires a resource before yielding it and supplies that yielded value to the operation.
Put resource release in a finally block surrounding yield so exit cleanup runs after successful use or an exception.
A yielding dependency defaults to request scope, ending after the response is sent; Depends(provider, scope="function") ends it after the handler finishes but before sending the response.
If a yielding dependency catches an exception without intentionally handling it, re-raise it rather than silently concealing the failure from FastAPI.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A request needs a resource that must be released afterward. A yielding dependency supplies the resource while keeping acquisition and release in one declared boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A dependency with yield acquires a resource before yielding it and supplies that yielded value to the operation.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Put resource release in a finally block surrounding yield so exit cleanup runs after successful use or an exception. A yielding dependency defaults to request scope, ending after the response is sent; Depends(provider, scope="function") ends it after the handler finishes but before sending the response. If a yielding dependency catches an exception without intentionally handling it, re-raise it rather than silently concealing the failure from FastAPI.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Acquire before yield and yield the resource to the operation. Put release in a finally block surrounding yield so cleanup covers successful use and exceptional exit. Trace two scopes: default request scope ends after the response is sent, while scope="function" ends after the handler finishes but before sending the response. Label handler completion and response sending separately on the timeline. If the dependency catches an exception it has not intentionally handled, re-raise it rather than hiding it from FastAPI. Resource cleanup and failure visibility must both remain clear. This lets you reason about when the supplied resource stops being owned by the dependency without treating yield as a generic promise of one cleanup time for all declarations.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A yielding dependency does not always end at handler completion. Default request scope and explicit function scope end at different points.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Release yield dependency resources: provide and close one request resource.

practice_anchor.objective: Implement a yielding provider that supplies one resource to an operation and closes it in finally. Compare default request scope with explicit function scope, and preserve any unhandled exception.
practice_anchor.success: The operation receives the yielded resource. Release runs on both successful and exceptional exits. Default request-scope cleanup occurs after response sending; function-scope cleanup occurs after handler completion but before response sending. Any caught, unhandled exception is re-raised.

live_code.required_skill: Enclose yield in try/finally, inject the yielded resource with Depends, and reason about cleanup timing and exception propagation.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Supply a resource acquisition callable, a resource with a close() method, and an operation scaffold with successful and exceptional paths. Leave the provider's yield/finally boundary and dependency declaration incomplete.
live_code.observable_success: For each execution path, the resource is supplied before operation use and closed at scope exit. An execution trace places closure after response sending for default request scope and before response sending for function scope. The exceptional path remains a failure rather than being silently swallowed.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show acquisition, yield, operation use, handler completion, response sending, and cleanup as separate events. Contrast default request scope with function scope, including successful and exceptional paths and re-raising an unhandled exception.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Yield encloses execution in a resource boundary.
Stay within the current objective: Release yield dependency resources. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Determine cleanup after success and failure.

context.concept_name: Structured service request and error logs

coverage.learning_objective: Emit structured diagnostics: add structured logs for one failure.

required_facts.statement: A useful event log records when and where an event happened, its type and severity, and enough context to interpret the event's outcome.
For a failure, record consistently named fields for timestamp, application or code location, event type, severity, result status and reason rather than an unexplained free-text message.

Emit logger.error(message, extra=event_fields) with the standard logging library to attach structured fields to the LogRecord, and configure the existing formatter or collection pipeline to preserve those field names; custom keys must not collide with reserved LogRecord attributes.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order failure logged only as "failed" tells the next developer very little. Structured event fields make the outcome interpretable without relying on unexplained free text.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A useful event log records when and where an event happened, its type and severity, and enough context to interpret the event's outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: For a failure, record consistently named fields for timestamp, application or code location, event type, severity, result status and reason rather than an unexplained free-text message. Emit logger.error(message, extra=event_fields) with the standard logging library to attach structured fields to the LogRecord, and configure the existing formatter or collection pipeline to preserve those field names; custom keys must not collide with reserved LogRecord attributes.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: For a synthetic failure, record consistently named fields for timestamp, code location, event type, severity, result status and reason. Pass the event fields using logger.error(message, extra=event_fields), then ensure the configured formatter or collector preserves them. Attaching fields to a LogRecord is only part of the path; inspect the emitted record as well. Use custom names that do not collide with reserved LogRecord attributes.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: An extra dictionary does not by itself establish that output preserves those fields. Check the formatter or collection pipeline.

video_need.reason: A tool demonstration can show the configured boundary and the evidence used to verify it. Focus: Emit structured diagnostics: add structured logs for one failure.

practice_anchor.objective: Add structured logging for one synthetic order failure using consistently named event fields, and configure the supplied formatter to preserve those fields.
practice_anchor.success: The emitted failure record preserves timestamp, code location, event type, severity, result status and reason under consistent field names. The logging call uses extra=event_fields, and custom keys do not collide with reserved LogRecord attributes.

live_code.required_skill: Construct an event-fields dictionary, attach it with the standard logging library, and preserve its fields through an existing formatter.
allowed_syntax: dictionary literals with string keys and string values
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an initialized logger, an existing handler and formatter, and a synthetic order failure currently logged only as 'failed'. Supply fixed failure values and the reserved-attribute reference. Learners add timestamp, code_location, event_type, event_severity, result_status and reason fields and update the existing formatter; the supplied runner captures the output.
live_code.observable_success: Running the supplied failure path produces an error-level record with all six event fields visible in the captured output. Each emitted field matches the synthetic failure, and no custom key overwrites a reserved LogRecord attribute.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the order failure's unexplained 'failed' output beside the structured output, with timestamp, code location, event type, severity, result status and reason visibly labeled. Connect the extra dictionary's keys to the fields preserved by the formatter.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Logs are structured event records.
Stay within the current objective: Emit structured diagnostics. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Identify insufficient failure logs.

context.concept_name: Preventing unsafe outbound requests and SSRF

coverage.learning_objective: Constrain outbound destinations: implement one destination policy.

required_facts.statement: When destinations are known, enforce a destination allowlist instead of allowing an untrusted value to choose an arbitrary outbound URL.
A destination policy must reject private, loopback, link-local and other non-public addresses, including IPv6 equivalents, when access is intended only to public services.
Validate the resolved address actually used for the connection, not merely a hostname checked earlier, to avoid a DNS rebinding gap.
Disable automatic redirects or apply the same destination checks to each redirect target so a permitted initial URL cannot redirect into a forbidden destination.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A service accepts destination-related input for an outbound lookup. If that input can select any URL, the service may be directed outside its intended public-service boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: When destinations are known, enforce a destination allowlist instead of allowing an untrusted value to choose an arbitrary outbound URL.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A destination policy must reject private, loopback, link-local and other non-public addresses, including IPv6 equivalents, when access is intended only to public services. Validate the resolved address actually used for the connection, not merely a hostname checked earlier, to avoid a DNS rebinding gap. Disable automatic redirects or apply the same destination checks to each redirect target so a permitted initial URL cannot redirect into a forbidden destination.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: When providers are known, map the request to an allowed destination instead of accepting an arbitrary URL. For public-only access, reject private, loopback, link-local and other non-public addresses, including IPv6 equivalents. Follow the connection beyond the first hostname check: validate the resolved address actually used, because an earlier hostname check alone leaves a DNS rebinding gap. Then trace a redirect from an initially permitted destination. Either disable automatic redirects or apply the same checks to each target. Work through requested destination, connected address and redirect target separately. A policy covering only the first stage is not the same boundary as one covering where the connection actually goes.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A permitted-looking hostname alone is insufficient. The connected address and redirect targets must respect the destination policy too.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Constrain outbound destinations: implement one destination policy.

practice_anchor.objective: Implement a destination allowlist that maps a requested provider to a fixed, approved destination and rejects unknown providers instead of treating their input as an outbound URL.
practice_anchor.success: Known provider values return only their configured destinations. Unknown provider values, including arbitrary URL strings, are rejected. This implements destination selection, not the separate connected-address and redirect checks.

live_code.required_skill: Use a fixed provider-to-destination mapping and reject input that is not an allowed mapping key.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a fixed allowed_destinations mapping containing provider names and approved public-service destination URLs, plus an unfinished destination_for_provider(provider: str) -> str function. Keep network connections outside this exercise.
live_code.observable_success: Calling the function with each configured provider returns its exact configured destination. Calling it with an unknown provider or an arbitrary URL raises ValueError rather than returning the supplied value.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the outbound trust boundary visible across three separate stages: requested provider mapped to an allowed destination, the resolved address actually used for the connection, and any redirect target. Mark private, loopback, link-local and other non-public IPv4 and IPv6 destinations as forbidden for public-only access, and show where each stage requires enforcement.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Untrusted input must not select privileged destinations.
Stay within the current objective: Constrain outbound destinations. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Identify SSRF network-trust violations.

context.concept_name: Bounded form and multipart file inputs

coverage.learning_objective: Accept bounded form and multipart inputs: implement one bounded multipart endpoint with form metadata and a file.

required_facts.statement: Declare form metadata with Annotated[Type, Form()] and an uploaded file with Annotated[UploadFile, File()] in the same multipart handler; multipart parsing requires python-multipart.
UploadFile uses a spooled file rather than requiring the entire upload to be represented as bytes in memory, and exposes asynchronous read, seek and close methods.
Apply RequestBodyLimitMiddleware with a finite max_body_size to count actual incoming body bytes, including multipart overhead, and return 413 when the limit is exceeded.

Multipart parsing can separately bound file count, field count and non-file field size with request.form(max_files=..., max_fields=..., max_part_size=...); these controls do not replace a total body limit.
Reject disallowed content types and validate the supplied fields before processing, then close an UploadFile with await file.close() when finished with its resource.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An upload endpoint accepts an attachment and form metadata. Multipart input is untrusted body data, so declaring UploadFile does not establish all resource limits.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Declare form metadata with Annotated[Type, Form()] and an uploaded file with Annotated[UploadFile, File()] in the same multipart handler; multipart parsing requires python-multipart.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: UploadFile uses a spooled file rather than requiring the entire upload to be represented as bytes in memory, and exposes asynchronous read, seek and close methods. Apply RequestBodyLimitMiddleware with a finite max_body_size to count actual incoming body bytes, including multipart overhead, and return 413 when the limit is exceeded. Multipart parsing can separately bound file count, field count and non-file field size with request.form(max_files=..., max_fields=..., max_part_size=...); these controls do not replace a total body limit. Reject disallowed content types and validate the supplied fields before processing, then close an UploadFile with await file.close() when finished with its resource.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Bind metadata with Form and the attachment with File and UploadFile, with python-multipart installed. UploadFile uses a spooled file and supports asynchronous resource methods. Configure RequestBodyLimitMiddleware with finite max_body_size for the supplied total body budget; incoming bytes include multipart overhead, and excess returns 413. Separately bound file count, field count and non-file field size through request.form options. Compare many small fields with an oversized total body: parser controls and total body limits answer different questions. Reject disallowed content types and validate fields before processing, then close the file when finished. Treat the body budget as actual bytes received, not an assumption based on how the caller describes the attachment.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A spooled upload is not an unlimited-input policy. Multipart parser limits also do not replace a total actual-body-byte limit.

video_need.reason: A tool demonstration can show the configured boundary and the evidence used to verify it. Focus: Accept bounded form and multipart inputs: implement one bounded multipart endpoint with form metadata and a file.

practice_anchor.objective: Implement one bounded attachment endpoint that binds form metadata and an uploaded file, enforces a finite total body budget and separate multipart parser limits, validates inputs before processing, and closes the uploaded file.
practice_anchor.success: The endpoint accepts permitted metadata and attachment content, rejects disallowed attachment content types and invalid metadata before processing, returns 413 when actual body bytes exceed the budget, applies the configured parser limits before binding, and closes every file resource it handles.

live_code.required_skill: Combine typed multipart binding, existing middleware configuration, bounded multipart parsing, input checks, and asynchronous file cleanup.
allowed_syntax: from fastapi import FastAPI, Form, File, UploadFile, Request, HTTPException
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an application scaffold, installed python-multipart, an importable RequestBodyLimitMiddleware implementation, and a pre-binding parsing scaffold that applies request.form limits before automatic parameter binding. Use only metadata and file as input names. Supply a finite body budget, parser budgets, permitted attachment content types, and a metadata length rule; leave endpoint binding, configuration values, validation, bounded reading, and cleanup unfinished.
live_code.observable_success: In the supplied execution harness, permitted metadata and file inputs reach processing; invalid metadata and disallowed attachment content types do not. An oversized actual body produces 413, including when multipart overhead pushes it over budget. Excess files, fields, or non-file field size are rejected by the parser boundary. The handler reads a bounded amount and closes its file on both successful processing and handler-level rejection.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the total-body middleware boundary, pre-binding multipart parser limits, typed metadata and file parameters, validation-before-processing order, and finally-based asynchronous file cleanup visible in one endpoint scaffold.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Multipart is an untrusted structured stream, not an unlimited in-memory value.
Stay within the current objective: Accept bounded form and multipart inputs. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Reject oversized or disallowed multipart data while binding form values and handling file resources safely.

coverage.learning_objective: Set safe CORS policy: configure one browser-client policy.

required_facts.statement: Configure app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=[...], allow_methods=[...], allow_headers=[...], allow_credentials=...) with the origins, methods and headers the browser client actually needs.
CORSMiddleware defaults are restrictive: allowed methods default to GET and credentials default to false.
When allow_credentials=True, explicitly specify allowed origins, methods and headers rather than wildcard lists.
CORS signals browser access permission; it does not replace access-control checks at API endpoints.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A browser client needs permission to call an API across origins. Configure for that client without confusing browser access with endpoint access control.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Configure app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=[...], allow_methods=[...], allow_headers=[...], allow_credentials=...) with the origins, methods and headers the browser client actually needs.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: CORSMiddleware defaults are restrictive: allowed methods default to GET and credentials default to false. When allow_credentials=True, explicitly specify allowed origins, methods and headers rather than wildcard lists. CORS signals browser access permission; it does not replace access-control checks at API endpoints.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: For a hypothetical client at https://shop.example, list that origin and the required methods and headers in CORSMiddleware configuration. Defaults are restrictive: methods default to GET and credentials to false. If credentialed access is needed, set allow_credentials=True and explicitly list origins, methods and headers rather than wildcards. Compare each policy dimension with the intended browser call. A matching origin alone does not explain whether the method and headers are allowed. After this browser-access policy is established, the API still needs endpoint access checks. Draw that as a separate boundary so middleware is not presented as a replacement for authentication or authorization.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: CORS grants browser response access, not caller authority. Credentialed configuration requires explicit origins, methods and headers.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Set safe CORS policy: configure one browser-client policy.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure CORSMiddleware for the browser client at https://shop.example, allowing GET and POST requests with the Content-Type header and credentialed browser access.
practice_anchor.success: The application registers CORSMiddleware with the exact client origin, explicit GET and POST methods, an explicit Content-Type header list, and allow_credentials=True, without wildcard entries.

live_code.required_skill: Translate one browser client's origin, method, header and credential requirements into an explicit CORSMiddleware policy.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide the FastAPI and CORSMiddleware imports and an app = FastAPI() declaration. State that https://shop.example needs GET, POST, Content-Type and credentialed browser access; leave middleware registration for the learner.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the CORSMiddleware declaration visible with annotations linking each explicit list and the credential flag to the shop client's requirements, alongside a separate boundary showing that browser access permission does not replace endpoint access checks.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: CORS controls browser response access, not authentication.

coverage.learning_objective: Control dependency reuse: verify one shared provider's identity.

required_facts.statement: FastAPI normally caches a dependency's returned value within one request when multiple dependants declare the same dependency.
Set Depends(provider, use_cache=False) when that declaration needs a fresh execution instead of the cached result.
Verify request-local reuse by having two dependants receive the same provider result during one request and checking a fresh request independently; this cache is not application-wide storage.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two providers in one request may need the same dependency result. FastAPI normally reuses it within the request, not as application-wide storage.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: FastAPI normally caches a dependency's returned value within one request when multiple dependants declare the same dependency.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Set Depends(provider, use_cache=False) when that declaration needs a fresh execution instead of the cached result. Verify request-local reuse by having two dependants receive the same provider result during one request and checking a fresh request independently; this cache is not application-wide storage.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Label the provider result for request A as value A. Have two dependants declare the same provider and verify reuse within A. Then send request B and inspect it independently rather than assuming value A is service-wide. If one declaration needs fresh execution, use Depends(provider, use_cache=False) there. Trace resolution with and without that setting to identify where another execution is required. The default cache reduces repeated dependency execution within a request; its boundary is that request, not all clients or worker processes. This matters when interpreting a provider returning a request-specific value.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Dependency caching is normally request-local. It is not a substitute for application-wide storage.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Control dependency reuse: verify one shared provider's identity.

practice_anchor.objective: Have two dependants declare the same provider, compare their received values by identity during one request, and repeat the check in a fresh request.
practice_anchor.success: Requests A and B each report that both dependants received the same instance. Provider execution records show one execution in A and a separate execution in B, establishing reuse within each request rather than across requests.

allowed_syntax: calls to the existing structured logger
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a running FastAPI application with a provider that constructs a new instance and records each execution through the existing structured logger. Include two dependants declaring that provider and an unfinished handler that compares their returned values. Use the provider and value terminology from the worked example.
live_code.observable_success: After completing the identity comparison, manually send request A and then request B. Each response reports true for shared identity, and the execution records show a separate provider execution for each request.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show separate boundaries for requests A and B. Within each boundary, trace one provider execution supplying the same instance to two dependants. Contrast a declaration using use_cache=False, which requires a fresh execution rather than reuse of the cached result.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Caching has request-local identity and lifetime.
Stay within the current objective: Control dependency reuse. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Predict reuse within one request.

context.concept_name: Endpoint integration tests using TestClient or async HTTPX as appropriate

coverage.learning_objective: Test an endpoint through its HTTP interface: write one integration test with TestClient or compatible async HTTPX setup.

required_facts.statement: Create TestClient(app), send an HTTP request with client.get(...) or another request method, and assert response.status_code and response.json() in a test_ function run by pytest.
Use with TestClient(app) as client when the test must execute application lifespan setup and teardown.
Sending a request through TestClient exercises the application's route and dependency resolution rather than only calling the handler function directly.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Calling a handler directly can miss routing or dependency problems. An endpoint integration test exercises the application's HTTP boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Create TestClient(app), send an HTTP request with client.get(...) or another request method, and assert response.status_code and response.json() in a test_ function run by pytest.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Use with TestClient(app) as client when the test must execute application lifespan setup and teardown. Sending a request through TestClient exercises the application's route and dependency resolution rather than only calling the handler function directly.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: A concrete test has an expected exchange, not just a call that did not crash. For a hypothetical order retrieval, name the request path and method, expected status, and expected public JSON fields. TestClient sends that request through the assembled application, so route and dependency resolution participate. If application setup matters, the context manager adds lifespan execution to the test boundary. A direct handler invocation may still be useful for another purpose, but it does not establish that the registered endpoint resolves its inputs and produces that HTTP exchange. Explain the boundary each test exercises before interpreting a successful assertion as broader evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content:
For a synthetic order-retrieval contract, GET /orders/42 should return status 200 and the JSON body {"id": 42, "quantity": 2}. With app configured for that contract, this test demonstrates both assertions:

```python
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

def test_get_order():
    with TestClient(app) as client:
        response = client.get("/orders/42")
        assert response.status_code == 200
        assert response.json() == {"id": 42, "quantity": 2}
```

Run the test_ function with pytest. The request goes through route and dependency resolution, unlike a direct handler call. The TestClient context executes lifespan setup and teardown when the case requires application-lifetime resources. The status assertion checks the intended HTTP outcome; the JSON assertion checks the expected public content. Neither assertion substitutes for the other.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A direct function call is not an HTTP endpoint test. Execute lifespan with the TestClient context when the case needs it.

video_need.reason: Running controlled success and failure cases makes the observable application boundary and assertions concrete. Focus: Test an endpoint through its HTTP interface: write one integration test with TestClient or compatible async HTTPX setup.

segments.label: Send a TestClient request and assert status and JSON
segments.summary: An endpoint test imports TestClient and the application, creates a client, and sends a GET request from a test function. It checks that the response status is 200 and the decoded JSON equals the string "server is running". Running pytest produces a passing test. Adding an exclamation mark to the endpoint's response makes the same test fail, demonstrating that the payload assertion detects a changed response. The original response is then restored.

context.concept_name: Required, optional and default input semantics

coverage.learning_objective: Define required, nullable and default inputs: test omitted, null and concrete values for one input.

required_facts.statement: Requiredness depends on whether a declaration supplies a default, while nullability depends on whether its type admits None.
A nullable field without a default still requires presence; writing field: Type | None = None permits both omission and an explicit null.
Test absence, an explicit JSON null and a concrete value as separate requests and compare them with the field's declared default and nullable type.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order note can be required to appear while allowing null as its value. Presence and nullability should not collapse into one "optional" case.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Requiredness depends on whether a declaration supplies a default, while nullability depends on whether its type admits None.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A nullable field without a default still requires presence; writing field: Type | None = None permits both omission and an explicit null. Test absence, an explicit JSON null and a concrete value as separate requests and compare them with the field's declared default and nullable type.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: A small presence table can have rows for missing, explicit null and concrete string. With a nullable field lacking a default, missing is not accepted as omission, while null is an admitted value. With a nullable field defaulting to None, both missing and null are allowed. The concrete string is checked against the declared type in either form. This comparison avoids overloading "optional" to mean several different things. Requiredness comes from whether the declaration supplies a default, and nullability comes from the admitted type. Keep both visible when reading or changing the contract.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Compare note: str | None without a default with note: str | None = None. The first requires presence but admits null. The second permits omission and explicit null. Send three bodies: one omitting note, one supplying null and one supplying a concrete note. Compare each with the declaration rather than treating them as interchangeable. For a field without a default, missing presence is the issue; for a nullable type, null is a permitted value. A two-axis table labeled presence and value keeps a default from being mistaken for a type choice. This clarifies the input contract before later partial-update behavior uses presence to express intent.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Nullable does not automatically mean omittable. A nullable field without a default still requires presence.

video_need.reason: A small comparison table makes the contrasting cases clear; a moving demonstration would mostly repeat the text. Focus: Define required, nullable and default inputs: test omitted, null and concrete values for one input.

practice_anchor.objective: Test three separate request bodies for note: an omitted field, explicit JSON null and a concrete string. Compare the results for note: str | None and note: str | None = None.
practice_anchor.success: Tests establish that the declaration without a default requires note to be present but accepts null or a string, while the declaration defaulting to None accepts all three inputs and uses None when note is omitted.

allowed_syntax: def path-operation functions with typed request-model parameters

After adding the None default, all three are accepted; the returned note is None for omission and null, and the supplied string for the concrete-value request.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show rows for omitted note, explicit null and a concrete string, with columns comparing acceptance and resulting value for note: str | None versus note: str | None = None. Keep presence requirements and admitted values separately visible.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Presence and nullability are independent contract dimensions.
Stay within the current objective: Define required, nullable and default inputs. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Distinguish omission from explicit null and supplied values.

context.concept_name: FastAPI OpenAPI generation from typed route contracts

coverage.learning_objective: Generate OpenAPI from declarations: inspect one endpoint schema.

required_facts.statement: FastAPI normally exposes the generated OpenAPI document at /openapi.json, describing the application's operations and data schemas.
Typed body declarations and response models contribute input and output schemas to the generated API contract.
Inspect the method entry under paths for an endpoint and follow its schema references into components to see the generated public input and output definitions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Typed declarations also describe the public API contract. Generated OpenAPI connects operation entries with the input and output schemas they contribute.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: FastAPI normally exposes the generated OpenAPI document at /openapi.json, describing the application's operations and data schemas.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Typed body declarations and response models contribute input and output schemas to the generated API contract. Inspect the method entry under paths for an endpoint and follow its schema references into components to see the generated public input and output definitions.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: The generated document has a navigation task as well as a content task. First locate the operation by path and method. Then follow its schema references to see the public field definitions contributed by body and response declarations. Finally compare those definitions with the declarations being taught. This lets a learner answer where the schema comes from and which operation uses it without assuming every detail appears in the operation entry itself. The document is a generated description of operations and data schemas; reading it is not the same as exercising every runtime path. Stay focused here on understanding that generated structure.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: An operation may reference schemas in components. Do not assume every field detail appears inline.

coverage.learning_objective: Enforce accepted HTTP hosts: configure one deployment host allowlist.

required_facts.statement: TrustedHostMiddleware validates the request Host against an allowed_hosts list and responds with 400 when the host is not allowed.
Configure app.add_middleware(TrustedHostMiddleware, allowed_hosts=[...]) using domain names; *.example.com permits subdomains and ["*"] permits any host.
www_redirect defaults to true and can redirect an allowed non-www host to its www counterpart, so account for it when verifying an allowlist's response.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A deployment should accept only intended request host identities. TrustedHostMiddleware checks this Host boundary independently of other metadata.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: TrustedHostMiddleware validates the request Host against an allowed_hosts list and responds with 400 when the host is not allowed.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Configure app.add_middleware(TrustedHostMiddleware, allowed_hosts=[...]) using domain names; *.example.com permits subdomains and ["*"] permits any host. www_redirect defaults to true and can redirect an allowed non-www host to its www counterpart, so account for it when verifying an allowlist's response.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Configure allowed_hosts with intended domain names. An unallowed Host gets 400. Compare an exact domain with *.example.com, permitting subdomains, and ["*"], permitting any host. These are different policies. Account for www_redirect, whose default true behavior can redirect an allowed non-www host to its www counterpart. In verification, record the supplied Host and observed response rather than assuming all allowed cases look identical. Trace rejection separately from an allowed redirect. This keeps requested host identity separate from authentication or trust in forwarded proxy metadata.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: An all-host wildcard removes the selective allowlist boundary. Allowed non-www cases may redirect under www_redirect.

context.concept_name: Credential and sensitive-data redaction from emitted logs

coverage.learning_objective: Redact sensitive logs: verify one failure's redaction.

required_facts.statement: Access tokens, passwords, primary secrets and sensitive personal data should usually not be recorded directly in logs; remove or mask them according to the logging policy.
Review diagnostic context as well as the main log message, because connection strings, session identifiers and other sensitive values can appear in supplemental fields.

Exercise a failure with recognizable synthetic sensitive values, inspect the emitted records and confirm that the redaction policy removes the prohibited values while retaining the intended event fields.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A useful diagnostic record must not expose credentials or personal information. Redaction covers supplemental context as well as the main message.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Access tokens, passwords, primary secrets and sensitive personal data should usually not be recorded directly in logs; remove or mask them according to the logging policy.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Review diagnostic context as well as the main log message, because connection strings, session identifiers and other sensitive values can appear in supplemental fields. Exercise a failure with recognizable synthetic sensitive values, inspect the emitted records and confirm that the redaction policy removes the prohibited values while retaining the intended event fields.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Exercise a synthetic failure with a recognizable fake token and fake connection-string secret. Inspect the full emitted record, including extra fields. Under the supplied logging policy, remove or mask prohibited values while retaining intended event fields. Success means the diagnostic remains interpretable without prohibited synthetic strings, not merely that the main message looks safe.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A safe message can still have unsafe context. Inspect the emitted record, not just the message template.

coverage.learning_objective: Own an async-compatible database session for a request: supply and close one async-compatible session per request.

required_facts.statement: AsyncSession maintains mutable state for current database work and is not safe to share across concurrent tasks; use a separate session for each concurrent unit of work.
Build an async_sessionmaker bound to an async engine and use async with session_factory() as session to obtain and close a session for the request's unit of work.
A request dependency can yield a session from its async context, leaving session cleanup to that context on both normal and exceptional exit.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A database session holds mutable state for current work. Concurrent requests should not become concurrent users of one shared session.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: AsyncSession maintains mutable state for current database work and is not safe to share across concurrent tasks; use a separate session for each concurrent unit of work.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Build an async_sessionmaker bound to an async engine and use async with session_factory() as session to obtain and close a session for the request's unit of work. A request dependency can yield a session from its async context, leaving session cleanup to that context on both normal and exceptional exit.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Separate the engine-bound factory from the individual session in your ownership sketch. The factory is used to obtain sessions, while an AsyncSession contains mutable state for current database work. Request A and request B should therefore have separate session boxes for concurrent work. Each async context owns closure even when the request fails. Yielding from that context supplies the session to the operation without removing the context cleanup responsibility. This makes the intended request unit of work visible instead of allowing all concurrent users to borrow one mutable object. Session creation and cleanup belong to the same ownership explanation.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Build an async_sessionmaker bound to the async engine. For each request unit of work, use async with session_factory() as session to obtain and close a session. A dependency can yield it from that context, preserving normal and exceptional cleanup. Draw request A with session A and request B with session B. They may share factory setup, but mutable sessions belong to separate concurrent work units. One application-wide session borrowed by both tasks violates this boundary. Follow ownership from creation through dependency use to context exit; cleanup should not depend solely on the successful return branch.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A shared factory is not permission to share one AsyncSession across concurrent tasks.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Own an async-compatible database session for a request: supply and close one async-compatible session per request.

coverage.learning_objective: Verify graceful shutdown: verify termination during one request.

required_facts.statement: Graceful server termination stops old processes accepting new connections and permits active responses and background tasks to finish within configured time limits.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A deployment terminates while an order request is active. Graceful shutdown is a bounded opportunity for work and cleanup, not indefinite waiting.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Graceful server termination stops old processes accepting new connections and permits active responses and background tasks to finish within configured time limits.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Configure --timeout-graceful-shutdown seconds as the maximum wait before Uvicorn starts terminating remaining requests. Verify termination during an active request by observing whether its response completes within the limit and whether lifespan cleanup releases the application's shared resources.

Terminate during a controlled active request and observe whether its response completes within that limit. Inspect whether lifespan cleanup releases shared resources. teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Graceful does not mean unlimited time or guaranteed completion. Verify response behavior and resource cleanup against the bound.

coverage.learning_objective: Design health probe contracts: specify one service's probes.

required_facts.statement: A failed liveness probe can cause a container restart, whereas a failed readiness probe removes its eligibility to receive service traffic without requiring a restart.
Readiness can depend on temporary conditions such as required backend availability, even while the process is alive.
Configure separate livenessProbe and readinessProbe HTTP checks with path, port, periodSeconds and failureThreshold that match the service's intended restart and traffic-eligibility contracts.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A process can be alive while unable to serve traffic because a required backend is temporarily unavailable. Liveness and readiness express different decisions.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A failed liveness probe can cause a container restart, whereas a failed readiness probe removes its eligibility to receive service traffic without requiring a restart.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Readiness can depend on temporary conditions such as required backend availability, even while the process is alive. Configure separate livenessProbe and readinessProbe HTTP checks with path, port, periodSeconds and failureThreshold that match the service's intended restart and traffic-eligibility contracts. An HTTP probe regards response status codes from 200 through 399 as success; other codes are failure.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Configure separate livenessProbe and readinessProbe HTTP checks with supplied path, port, periodSeconds and failureThreshold. Trace a backend outage while the process remains alive: readiness can remove traffic eligibility without requiring restart. Failed liveness can cause restart. HTTP probes classify 200 through 399 as success, other codes as failure. Compare this with the intended probe contract; calling a body "unready" is not enough if its status still counts as successful. Draw restart and traffic eligibility separately so a dependency outage is not automatically treated as proof that restarting is intended.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Alive does not necessarily mean ready. HTTP probe success includes 3xx, not just 200.
